title: Romanian Deadlift
summary: A hip hinge from standing with soft knees: the hamstrings work from a deep stretch with the glutes and lower back helping. Hamstrings 1, glutes and lower back 0.7.

muscles.why: Pushing the hips back bends the hip with the knee almost fixed, so the hamstrings lengthen under load and then extend the hip to stand up.
The glutes extend the hip with the hamstrings, most near the bottom where the hip is most bent.
The spinal erectors hold the back flat against a long lever; isometric but hard work, rated 0.7.
You hold the bar the whole set, so grip is real work and can limit the set (swap tag 'More grip demand').
The adductor magnus also extends the hip, so it helps.
Upper traps hold the shoulders against the bar's pull: minor.
The lats keep the bar close to the legs: minor.
Mid-back holds the shoulders set: minor.
Hip muscles steady the pelvis: minor.

setup.text: Start from a rack or deadlift the bar up first, feet hip width.
Grip just outside the thighs; straps are fine if grip runs out first.
Stand tall, soften the knees and set your back flat.

form_cues.why: The hips moving back is what lengthens the hamstrings.

form_cues.cue: Keep the bar close to your legs
form_cues.why: A close bar keeps the lever arm short for the lower back.

form_cues.cue: Stop at a deep hamstring stretch and stand up
form_cues.why: Stopping where your back stays flat keeps the stretch in the hamstrings.

form_cues.cue: The movement is hips back, not bending down. Your knee angle barely changes.
form_cues.why: If the knees bend more, it becomes a deadlift and the hamstrings get shorter.
Keeps the bar path vertical and close.

bias_tweaks.change: Go deeper only as far as the back stays flat
bias_tweaks.effect: More hip bend, more hamstring stretch.
bias_tweaks.caveat: Depth is limited by hamstring length; mid-shin is typical.

bias_tweaks.effect: Lets you go deeper at the hip, with more glute and less hamstring stretch.
bias_tweaks.caveat: Too much knee bend turns it into a conventional deadlift.

bias_tweaks.effect: Removes grip as the limit so the hamstrings reach a hard set.
bias_tweaks.caveat: Train grip separately if you want it.

mistakes.text: Rounding the back to reach the bar lower.
mistakes.fix: Stop where your back starts to round; that is your current depth.

mistakes.text: Squatting the bar down by bending the knees a lot.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knee angle almost fixed; hips back.

mistakes.text: Letting the bar drift forward away from the legs.
mistakes.fix: Drag the bar down the thighs.

mistakes.text: Looking up hard and over-arching at the top.

misconceptions.myth: The RDL is a lower-back exercise.
misconceptions.reality: The hamstrings and glutes are the main movers; the lower back holds position (rated 0.7).

misconceptions.myth: Every set has to go to failure to grow.
misconceptions.reality: Stopping a few reps short gave similar growth to failure in a meta-analysis; growth tends to rise as sets get closer to failure, but the exact curve is uncertain.

lower_risk.text: Ramp up before your first working set. For primary lifts the app suggests 50% x 8, 70% x 4 and 85% x 2 when the first working load is 60 kg or more, and 50% x 8 then 75% x 3 below that.
lower_risk.note: High-load warm-ups improved strength performance in a systematic review; the percentages are coaching convention.

lower_risk.text: Add load in small steps. The app suggests a heavier load only when the jump is 5% or less; otherwise it adds a rep first, up to 2 past the top of the range. Default steps for this equipment are 2.5 kg or 5 lb; your gym profile can replace them.
Aim for about 3 reps in reserve in the 6-10 rep range. With a heavy barbell hinge, stay a little further from failure; end the set when you can't keep the back flat.
Lower under control to your flat-back depth every rep; no bouncing at the bottom.
Start from a rack at hip height or pull from the floor with good form; set the bar down rather than dropping it from a rounded position.
Pick a variation, range and setup you can train comfortably.

alternatives.why: The landmine path takes some load off the spine and is easier to learn.
Same hinge with dumbbells; less load to handle.
Hamstrings at the knee with no back or grip demand; grew the hamstrings well when the hip is bent.
Hip-extension work with far less load and fatigue; hip-extension training grew the hamstrings in a 10-week study.
Bar on the back, so grip is not a limit; harder to learn.

notes: Hinge ratings are a model; hamstring growth from RDLs specifically is not compared to curls in a study the app cites.
Ratings and display bands are the library model (main >= 0.75, helper 0.4 to < 0.75, minor 0.25 to < 0.4, not counted < 0.25).
Technique and load management only. This page makes no medical or injury claims.
